We propose embedding life-cycle assessment and transformation risk metrics into future technology evaluations, providing a structured, carbon-aware roadmap for next-generation water engineering. Ultimately, this unified paradigm aims to redefine water purification infrastructure, transitioning it from a conventional end-of-pipe remediation asset into a core engine of circular regeneration and value creation.

title: A planetary health approach is needed to manage the wider impacts of rice production
abstract: Rice production is critical to global food security, but it has unintended consequences: water stress, greenhouse gas emissions and disease-vector mosquitoes and snails, usually addressed by separate sectors in isolation. A planetary health approach that integrates agriculture, water, climate, ecosystems and health can identify rice growing practices that deliver benefits across these domains.

title: Ice–water interfaces drive speciation transformation and suppress bioavailability potential of freshly deposited arsenic during soil freeze–thaw cycles
abstract: Ubiquitous freeze–thaw cycles serve as a hidden driver reshaping arsenic (As) bioavailability in industrial and adjacent agricultural soils impacted by industrial emissions. Here we show that ice–water interfaces trigger rapid changes in the speciation and bioavailability potential of freshly deposited As particles in soils, primarily within the first three freeze–thaw cycles. Many industrial parks and nearby farmlands are located in regions with subzero temperatures that coincide with or follow precipitation, frequently inducing freeze–thaw events. These conditions reduced the As relative leachability ratio (unfrozen before) by an average of 71% in 50 diverse soil samples from across China. Quasi-in situ and single-particle analysis unveiled As transformations into relatively stable forms (for example, ferric arsenate and haematite-associated As) during freeze–thaw cycles. Beyond typical environmental factors, concentration effects induced fluctuations in chemistry in the microenvironment of ice boundaries that steered speciation changes, while physical fragmentation redistributed As mass across particle-size fractions. This study reveals the previously overlooked role of natural freeze–thaw dynamics in altering the speciation and reactivity of freshly deposited heavy metal particles in cold and wet conditions, providing new insights into their initial geochemical fate following industrial emission.

title: Quantifying the global potential of solar-driven interfacial evaporation using a validated climate–performance model
abstract: Solar-driven interfacial evaporation (SDIE) offers sustainable pathways for water, food, sterilization and mining, advancing Sustainable Development Goals. However, assessing its real-world potential remains challenging because SDIE performance, resource availability and demand all vary across space and time. Here we develop experimentally validated climate–performance models and integrate them with high-resolution climatic, hydrological and socioeconomic datasets to quantify global SDIE potential. Specifically, an open-source, extensible geospatial toolset SDIE-Geo is developed to map SDIE performance at hourly resolution and align it with local resource availability, demand and socioeconomic context to reveal deployment potential. Key SDIE-based applications advancing Sustainable Development Goals include year-round sterilization in Niger, drinking water provision for 1 billion people at 2 l per day with a 0.7-m 2 device and accelerating lithium-brine concentration by up to 135-fold. These findings provide quantitative guidance for SDIE deployment and design, and establish a general framework for evaluating climate-sensitive technologies at the global scale.

title: Synergistic water and mineral harvesting from seawater
abstract: Solar desalination is a promising technology for freshwater production. Coupling solar-driven interfacial evaporation with selective ion adsorption for the concurrent recovery of freshwater, lithium, and uranium provides a sustainable paradigm for managing the water–energy–resource nexus.

title: China’s centralized wastewater treatment system reaches efficiency limits in tackling water scarcity
abstract: Centralized wastewater treatment systems (CWTSs) are increasingly expected to strengthen water security through reclaimed water reuse. Yet whether centralized expansion can simultaneously achieve cost recovery and reduce water stress remains unresolved. We assess the viability of CWTSs in China using an inventory of 10,826 wastewater treatment plants and data on wastewater generation, reuse demand and socioeconomic scenarios. Here we show that CWTS benefits are spatially bounded: only approximately 0.45 billion people live in areas where reclaimed water reuse can achieve cost recovery and reduce local water stress. Under prevailing fees of 0.9–1.1 Chinese yuan m − 3 , cost recovery requires plants to reach break-even scales of 6,793–49,744 m 3 per day. Projected urbanization does not substantially expand viable reuse opportunities, leaving 95–99% of prospective plants in unserved areas below break-even scale. Hybrid centralized–decentralized systems can meet national targets at 25–37% lower cost. These findings support a transition from purely centralized to coordinated hybrid systems in developing regions.

title: Water science is more than papers
abstract: Water science should be our collective capacity to turn knowledge into tangible solutions. Yet the current reward system prioritizes scientific output over translation, leaving society increasingly vulnerable to escalating water crises.

title: Atmospheric drying translates unevenly into river drought
abstract: Climate warming is increasing atmospheric evaporative demand and strengthening some measures of drought, but the consequences for water availability depend on how this climate signal propagates through terrestrial water systems. An analysis of nearly 19,000 catchments shows that river-flow drought responds heterogeneously, underscoring the need to match drought assessments to the impacts of interest.

title: Risk-financing systems must adapt to a changing hydrological reality
abstract: Hydrological extremes are intensifying faster than risk-financing systems can adapt, pushing vulnerable countries towards a resilience trap. Closing the financial protection gap for water-related disasters will require action across four areas: anticipation, inclusion, prevention and mutualization.

title: Water treatment research opportunities at synchrotron and neutron user facilities
abstract: X-ray and neutron sources have driven major advancements in our understanding of the chemistry, structure and function of materials ranging from biomolecules to batteries. User facilities make these complex and costly-to-operate tools accessible to researchers. Yet these facilities remain underutilized by the water treatment community. Here we describe how these techniques have advanced water treatment research and highlight opportunities to develop transformative solutions via experiments that leverage user-facility infrastructure and capabilities (for example, in situ and operando sample environments and advanced computational modelling). Expanding user bases at these facilities will accelerate the molecular-level design of next-generation water treatment systems, including membranes for brine management, catalysts for contaminant degradation, and sorbents for resource recovery. Investigating dynamic structures and chemical heterogeneities under realistic operational conditions can reveal complex nanoscale processes such as partitioning or fouling that govern macroscopic performance. Such insights bridge laboratory-scale discoveries to system-level improvements, ultimately strengthening global water, resource and energy security.

title: Comparative analysis of selective ion removal in electrochemical technologies reveals the need for a new data representation framework
abstract: Ion-selective separations are essential for water treatment and resource circularity, yet conventional selectivity metrics provide limited practical value. We present an integrative framework that standardizes the evaluation across different separation technologies, where selectivity, purity and water recovery can be visualized on a single plot. To demonstrate the necessity of this framework, we analyse the selective performance of electrodialysis and membrane capacitive deionization (MCDI), and we reveal their different selective separation behaviour. We further identify two advantages unique to MCDI: (1) electrode-enhanced selectivity and (2) cyclic operation enabling infinite selectivity, allowing complete removal of target ions while achieving zero removal of competing ions, based on distinct ions’ absorption/desorption dynamics. By mapping electrodialysis and MCDI separation results using the proposed framework, we demonstrate the advantages of a flexible analysis of different removal regimes in a concise manner and a unified visualization of selectivity and removal/recovery ratios.

title: Realizing the human right to water means moving from remedy to prevention
abstract: The human right to water is well established in law, but putting it into practice remains difficult across diverse hydrological, social and governance contexts. A proactive, contextual approach can link water-security and governance conditions to challenges in realizing the right. This can help to anticipate problems before harm occurs and strengthen existing due-diligence and stewardship processes.

title: Author Correction: Fifty years of research have deepened uncertainties in global irrigation water withdrawals
Carbonation of silicate minerals contributes to atmospheric CO2 drawdown in glacier-fed streams
abstract: Glaciers produce abundant grains of reactive minerals that influence inorganic carbon cycling, yet the links between mineral weathering and CO 2 dynamics in glacier-fed streams (GFSs) remain poorly understood. Here we combine streamwater geochemistry, solute end-member modelling, carbonate saturation calculations and suspended-sediment mineralogy across 170 GFSs worldwide. We show that 69% of GFSs were undersaturated with respect to atmospheric CO 2 equilibrium, indicating widespread atmospheric CO 2 uptake. Grain-scale analyses of selected carbonate-bearing GFSs reveal metastable Mg-bearing carbonate phases consistent with secondary mineral formation in transient microenvironments. We propose that CO 2 released during sulfuric acid-driven carbonate weathering and secondary calcite precipitation can be partly consumed by carbonation of silicate- and clay-derived mineral surfaces, transferring dissolved inorganic carbon into particulate inorganic carbon. This sediment-mediated pathway can contribute to CO 2 undersaturation under favourable lithological and geochemical conditions, revealing a previously underappreciated coupling between chemical weathering, sediment–water interactions and inorganic carbon storage in proglacial landscapes rapidly expanding under global glacier retreat.

title: Solar-operated interlayer electrothermal evaporator enabling instant high-flux freshwater production across multiple scenarios
abstract: As conflicts and frequent natural disasters intensify, timely access to freshwater from multiple resources is extremely important for human survival. Electrothermal desalination is a promising solution for the development of green energy-driven, miniaturized and high-flux systems. However, traditional electrothermal desalination suffers from significant heat loss, which limits the improvement of the apparent energy efficiency, resulting in excessive energy consumption and a reliance on bulky equipment. Here we present an interlayer electrothermal evaporator (IEE) that reduces heat loss and energy consumption by nearly two-thirds compared with a bulk electrothermal evaporator. When the photothermal effect of solar energy is considered, the IEE attains an impressive apparent energy efficiency of 93.31% with a freshwater flux of 69.46 l m −2 h −1 . Significantly, the IEE uses solar cells to supply green electricity and incorporates a Fresnel lens for solar energy concentration, constituting a portable freshwater production system for outdoor application. The device produces 1.64 l of freshwater within 8 h with an evaporator area of only 30.72 cm 2 , which is sufficient to meet the daily needs of individuals, even from challenging water sources such as sediment water, oily water, high-salinity wastewater and strongly acidic water. Therefore, this green energy-driven IEE system enables high-flux freshwater production across diverse scenarios, providing a sustainable and scalable solution to mitigate freshwater scarcity.

title: Sustainable photoelectrochemical lithium extraction mediated by self-regulated potential
abstract: The rising demand for lithium poses substantial challenges in its extraction and recycling, stemming from the low concentrations of traditional lithium sources in specific geographical regions. By contrast, lithium reserves found in unconventional aqueous sources such as low-grade brines and seawater, are globally distributed but difficult to exploit due to competing ions and high energy demands. Here, to overcome these obstacles, we introduce a membrane-free photoelectrochemical strategy that enables direct and selective lithium extraction from seawater and low-grade brines using solar energy by a self-regulated electrode potential. This approach leverages a TiO 2 photoanode that generates a photovoltage directly coupled to lithium intercalation in a modified FePO 4 cathode. Owing to the dynamic balance between photogenerated charge carriers and interfacial redox kinetics, the cathode potential spontaneously stabilizes within the thermodynamic window for Li + intercalation, while remaining inaccessible to competing ions, particularly Na + . This intrinsic potential self-regulation eliminates the need for ion-selective membranes, external bias or reference electrodes, thereby simplifying the system architecture while preserving high lithium selectivity. As a result, the membrane-free photoelectrochemical platform enables stable and selective lithium extraction from seawater, low-grade brines and desalination brines, achieving a maximum uptake rate of 300 μg cm −2 h −1 . This study offers insights into solar-driven ion transport that could substantially advance global resource sustainability.

title: Freshwater needs its own treaty
abstract: As critical freshwater systems cross irreversible thresholds, governance remains fragmented across climate, biodiversity and desertification agreements. A dedicated scientific panel and a future Water COP could provide the framework needed to manage a water-constrained world.

title: Wastewater surveillance captures multi-marker responses to short-term examination stress in a university population
abstract: Young people frequently experience academic stress that may affect mental health and coping behaviours, yet population-level monitoring relies on self-reports or prescription data with limited temporal resolution. Here we use wastewater surveillance to assess short-term, multi-system stress dynamics in a university population. Wastewater samples collected in 2022 from an Australian campus (~30,000 people) were analysed for oxidative stress biomarkers, antidepressants, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medication and behavioural indicators including alcohol, nicotine and tobacco biomarkers, paraxanthine (caffeine biomarker) and acesulfame. Temporal patterns during examination period were compared with teaching periods and a contemporaneous general-population catchment (~120,000 residents). Difference-in-differences analysis showed a marked university-specific increase in 8-hydroxyguanine (8-OHG), weaker evidence for 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) and consistent but non-significant positive antidepressant consumption trends during examination period. Ritalinic acid and amphetamine, total nicotine and tobacco-derived nicotine, and alcohol remained relatively stable, whereas paraxanthine and acesulfame significantly decreased. By integrating multiple biomarkers, wastewater surveillance provides a non-invasive and complementary tool for identifying periods of increased mental health burden and informing timely public health interventions in university populations.
